TUTORIAL_4_Quick_classification_and_interpretation

Source: vignettes/TUTORIAL_4_Quick_classification_and_interpretation.Rmd
TUTORIAL_4_Quick_classification_and_interpretation.Rmd

The iPastoralist wrappers provide an optional shortcut for inspecting vegetation groups together with the ten most abundant species beside each survey. This can help reveal changes in species composition along the dendrogram and give each group an initial ecological interpretation.

Two functions are available: plotClustAggregate_twspn() for a TWINSPAN classification, illustrated here with phytosociological cover data, and plotClustAggregate() for agglomerative clustering, illustrated with point-quadrat data.

With aggregate = TRUE, both functions retain individual surveys as leaves, prefix their labels with group identifiers, draw rectangles around groups, and return a table describing group composition. Here, aggregation refers to the group summaries; surveys remain visible in the dendrogram.

Before running the examples

These examples complement the phytosociological and pastoral classification vignettes. Run each section after preparing the inputs in the corresponding workflow. The code is shown without automatic execution because it uses those existing objects and includes file export.

Use a version of iPastoralist containing the wrappers and their helper functions. The TWINSPAN wrapper also requires ecan::twinspan().

library(iPastoralist)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'vegan':
#>   method     from      
#>   rev.hclust dendextend

data_example <- as.data.frame(iPastoralist::data)
vegetation <- data_example[, c(2, 7:ncol(data_example))]
sra <- vegetation_abundance(
  database = vegetation,
  method = "SRA_fo"
)
# For subsequent analyses: rows = surveys; columns = species.
veg <- t(as.matrix(sra))

In both sections, veg is a numeric matrix with surveys in rows and species in columns, with unique survey and species names. Its meaning depends on the workflow: percentage cover for phytosociological surveys and SRA for the point-quadrat example. The object n.cluster is the chosen number of groups.

Two arguments control how many species are reported:

Argument Meaning Value used here
nspePlot Species appended to each survey label, ranked by abundance within that survey 10
aggr.Nspe Species reported for each group, ranked by mean abundance across its surveys 10

The first ten species beside a survey and the first ten species in a group summary describe different levels of the data. Both settings can be reduced independently when shorter labels or summaries are useful.

Phytosociological surveys: TWINSPAN 

phyto_groups <- plotClustAggregate_twspn(
  dbClust = veg,
  nspePlot = 10,
  aggregate = TRUE,
  aggr.Nspe = 3,
  modified = TRUE,
  n_clusters = 4,
  cut_levels = c(1, 2, 2, 40),
  min_size = 2,
  max_depth = 6,
  polish = "hill",
  species = FALSE,
  labels.cex = 0.5,
  clust.mar = c(1, 2, 2, 30),
  save.file = FALSE,
  display = TRUE
)


knitr::kable(phyto_groups)

Point-quadrat surveys: agglomerative clustering

Use the SRA matrix veg and the ranked-species table first10 prepared in the pastoral workflow. The table must contain the matching survey identifiers, Survey.order, and at least ten ranked-species columns, as returned by first_ten_species(..., join.dendrogram = TRUE, cluster.hclust = clst). The argument is spelled firt10 in the wrapper.

The following example uses Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and average linkage (UPGMA). It computes that classification from veg; its groups may differ from a chord-distance classification explored earlier. Choose the number of groups for the classification being displayed.

pq_groups <- plotClustAggregate(
  dbClust = veg,
  nspePlot = 10,
  distance = "chord",
  clust.method = "average",
  aggregate = TRUE,
  n.clust = 4,
  aggr.Nspe = 10,
  labels.cex = 0.5,
  clust.mar = c(1, 2, 2, 30),
  file.name = "point_quadrat_groups.pdf",
  file.height = 12,
  file.width = 24,
  save.file = F,
  format = "pdf"
)

knitr::kable(pq_groups)
group name
1 Fesnigr (13%), Phlrhae (8%), Agrcapi (6%), Triflav (5%), Chahirs (4%), Antalpi (4%), Alcvulg (4%), Rumalpe (4%), Vacmyrt (3%), Poaalpi (3%)
2 Descesp (43%), Carclav (11%), Phlrhae (9%), Fesnigr (8%), Poaalpi (6%), Alcvulg (4%), Peuostr (4%), Verlobe (4%), Rumalpe (2%), Caramar (1%)
3 Rhoferr (42%), Calvill (17%), Vacmyrt (9%), Junnana (8%), Rubidae (5%), Alnviri (5%), Fesscab (5%), Aveflex (4%), Gymdryo (2%), Arnmont (1%)
4 Alnviri (34%), Adealli (9%), Agrcapi (7%), Rubidae (6%), Urtdioi (5%), Viobifl (5%), Rumalpe (5%), Calvill (4%), Rhoferr (3%), Vacmyrt (3%)

Open aggregate_point_quadrat_groups.pdf in the working directory to inspect the groups and their survey labels. With the supplied implementation, save.file = FALSE computes the summary without drawing the grouped dendrogram, so file export is used here to view it.

The ranked species beside each survey report SRA, while the returned group and name columns describe the ten species with the highest mean SRA in each group. The wrapper recomputes clustering from the input matrix; the order stored in first10 does not supply an existing tree.

Reading the overview

Use the species appended to survey labels to inspect compositional variation within and between groups. Use the returned group summaries to identify the species contributing most strongly to mean composition. These abundance rankings do not measure species fidelity or statistical significance; diagnostic species require the corresponding analyses.

Group means include zero values for species absent from a survey. The summary text rounds means to whole numbers and appends a percent sign, without converting the input values to percentages. Use percentage cover or percentage SRA when interpreting those labels. Very small positive means may be displayed as 0%, and zero-mean species can occur at the end of a summary if fewer than ten species have positive means.

Ten species can make survey labels long. Increase the output width or right margin, or set nspePlot = 5 while keeping aggr.Nspe = 10 to retain a fuller group summary with a more compact dendrogram.
